Mr. Ash drove the screaming Elm to the warehouse rendezvous, cradled his bleeding body on the concrete ramp, and swore under his breath that he was not going to die today. 

Before the bleeding, the job had collapsed within a minute. Ash had shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Elm beside him. Fleeing on foot through residential backstreets, Elm hijacked a car, only for the terrified woman driving it to pull a pistol from the door pocket and shoot him in the stomach. Elm shot her dead, pulled himself into the driver’s seat, and bled all over the steering wheel as he sped away.

Inside the warehouse, Mr. Birch arrived clean, breathless, and furious. He argued that the job was a setup with an informer inside the crew, then slipped outside to hide the diamonds where no watching eyes could find them. 

Moments later, Ren Vasco strolled in unhurried. Ren produced a kidnapped patrolman, Doyle, dragging him bound and gagged from the boot of his car. 

It was a strange crew, assembled over cheap diner coffee. Over breakfast, eight men in black suits had sat around a table arguing about what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved a tip. Later in Bram's office, Bram handed out the tree aliases, and Mr. Birch had loudly objected to being called Mr. Birch. 

Left alone with the bound officer in the warehouse, Ren turned up a radio oldie playing on a nearby workbench. He danced a few light steps, took off Doyle’s ear with a razor, and then doused the screaming officer in petrol. 

From the floor, barely conscious, Elm lifted his gun and shot Ren dead. As Ren fell, Elm gasped out to Doyle that he was a cop, and that the police were already waiting outside for Bram.

Months before the warehouse, undercover officer Danny Roarke had sat in an empty safe room rehearsing a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet with his handler Pruitt until he could tell it like a real memory. Danny performed the anecdote effortlessly for Bram, his son Cal, and Mr. Ash in a dark bar, earning a laugh in the right place and getting taken onto the crew as Mr. Elm. Around the same time, Ren Vasco had walked out of prison after keeping his mouth shut for years, reporting directly to Bram and Cal, who owed him for his silence and put him on the diamond job.

Cal returned to the warehouse floor, listened to Elm’s breathless account of killing Ren, and accepted the story—then casually put three rounds into Doyle to close the matter forever.

Bram arrived last. He walked past the bodies, looked down at Elm, and flatly named him as the police informer. Ash refused to believe his boss, drew his gun, and pointed it at Bram to protect the man he had carried inside.

The three-way standoff detonated instantly. Bram, Cal, and Ash all fired at once. When the deafening echoes died, Bram and Cal lay still, leaving only Ash and Elm breathing on the red-stained floor.

Bleeding out beside him, Elm looked up into Ash's face and finally confessed that he was a police officer. Ash stared at him in horror, dragged himself up, and put his revolver to Elm's head. As the warehouse doors crashed inward and police stormed the room, Ash pulled the trigger, and a volley of automatic fire cut him down where he knelt.

A cardiologist shows Aaron Vale the numbers, explaining that his failing heart will kill him in weeks without a donor. In a sunlit house, Lena Ward lives a settled life with her husband Doug and two daughters, surrounded by children's drawings on the walls. On a Saturday afternoon, Wes Tarrow coaches boys' baseball, his forearms heavy with scripture tattoos, while his wife Nita watches his born-again fervor and dangerous temper with quiet dread.

In a car park, Aaron pays a private investigator to find the identity of the dead donor whose heart now beats inside his chest. Behind a roadside motel, Aaron holds a bought pistol against Wes, but his hand shakes; the shot only wounds the man, and Aaron tells him to run. In a hospital corridor, Lena sits in a side room as a doctor tells her that Doug and both of her young daughters are dead. 

At a pedestrian crossing, Wes’s pickup strikes Doug and the two girls; he stops, reverses briefly, and flees the scene. Later, Wes walks into a police station, confesses to the hit-and-run, and is sent back to prison. In an operating theatre, Doug’s heart is transplanted into Aaron, who wakes up breathing easily for the first time in months.

In her kitchen, Della presses Aaron to sign a consent form for her to be inseminated with his frozen sperm before he dies. In a locked bathroom, Lena returns to cocaine, beginning a methodical campaign of self-destruction. Released early from prison, Wes walks past his waiting family at the gate, abandoning his faith, and takes a room-cleaning job at a distant motel.

Aaron follows Lena to a public swimming pool, arranges a meeting, and begins an affair with her. In Lena’s kitchen, Aaron confesses that he carries her dead husband’s heart; she throws him out in rage, only to call him back four days later. Meanwhile, Aaron leaves Della, telling her he will not return and does not want the child she seeks to conceive.

Lena demands that the man who killed her family be dead, driving Aaron to track Wes down at the motel. After the failed shooting, a bleeding Wes follows Aaron and Lena into their motel room, begging Aaron to finish the job; instead, Aaron turns the gun on himself and shoots his own chest. 

At the hospital, surgeons try to save Aaron, but the transplanted heart fails on the table. Wes finally returns home to Nita and his family. Lena, now carrying Aaron's child, walks home alone.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war sat a young boy down in a bare front room, placing into Denny’s small hands the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity. Decades later, hiding in a cheap motel room on the edge of town, Denny asked his girlfriend Marielle whether she had packed it. She had left it on the bedside table of his flat. Denny returned to the flat anyway, retrieved the watch from the table, and found a hitman stepping out of the bathroom; reaching the submachine gun lying on the kitchen counter first, Denny shot Rollo dead. Hours later, with the watch fastened tightly back to his wrist, Denny collected Marielle, put her on the back of a motorcycle taken from a pawnshop, and rode out of the city for good.

Rollo and Marcus had driven across the city earlier that morning debating foreign drug laws and European fast food names without mentioning their errand. Waiting in the corridor outside their target’s flat, they argued whether giving a mobster's wife a foot massage was worth being thrown off a balcony. Inside, Marcus recited scripture to a terrified young man named Tobin before he and Rollo shot him for double-crossing their employer, Otis, and took back a heavy briefcase. A fourth man suddenly burst from the bathroom, emptying a revolver at six feet; every round missed, leaving Marcus standing unharmed against bullet-riddled plaster, calling his survival divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo’s gun accidentally went off over a bump, blowing passenger Del’s head off and painting the interior red. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren’s garage, where a soft-spoken fixer timed the cleanup to the minute, hosed both hitmen down in the yard, and dressed them in borrowed shorts and T-shirts. Stopping for breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner. When they reached Marcus's booth, he handed over his wallet, recited his passage, kept the briefcase, and talked the couple into walking out peaceful. Wearing their ridiculous clothes, Marcus and Rollo delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar, arriving while Otis was paying an ageing Denny to take a dive in the fifth.

Before that night out, Rollo drove to his dealer Kip’s house, bought a bag of pure heroin, and shot up at the kitchen table. He then escorted Otis's wife Nadia to a themed restaurant where waiters played vintage stars; the two took off their shoes and won the dance contest. Back at the flat, Nadia found Rollo's stash, mistook the powder for cocaine, snorted a line, and went blue on the carpet; Rollo rushed her to Kip's living room, reviving her only by driving a needle of adrenaline straight into her chest. Meanwhile, Denny broke his deal with Otis, winning his fight and hitting his opponent hard enough to kill him in the ring before escaping in a passing taxi. After collecting his watch from his flat, Denny’s car collided with Otis in the street, wrecking both vehicles and sending both men into the basement of a pawnshop, held captive by its owners. Denny broke free of his restraints, reached the street door, but returned with a sword taken off the shop wall while one captor was raping Otis. Denny killed the captors, and Otis declared them square on the condition Denny left town forever.

Behind a desk, insurance investigator Martin Kray denies the claim of a soft-spoken man named Elias Prine, ruling his severe memory loss purely psychosomatic. At home, Prine’s skeptical wife tests her husband by advancing her watch and repeatedly asking for her diabetic injections; unable to retain the past, Elias gives her dose after dose until she dies of an overdose.

Martin enters a parlour with a scribbled note and has a vehicle registration inked into his thigh beneath five permanent facts, trusting the needle over a head that resets every few minutes.

Night intruders burst into Martin’s bathroom, leaving his wife dead. Martin kills one attacker before taking a blow to the mirror, losing the ability to form new memories. To function, he constructs a rigid system of annotated instant photographs, clipped notes, and tattoos to hunt the surviving accomplice, known only as R.M.

At her bar, Corinne watches a stranger step out of a sports car wearing her missing boyfriend Gil’s suit. Recognizing the clothes and car, she smiles, takes Martin’s order, and quietly has her staff spit in his beer.

A year prior, a plainclothes officer named Roy led Martin to a derelict building, standing by while Martin shot the real attacker dead—a vengeance Martin forgot within minutes. Later, Martin burns his wife’s hairbrush and paperbacks in an open field, unable to hold his grief long enough to finish it.

Inside her house, Corinne hides every pen before goading Martin into striking her. Returning bruised, she blames a man named Vance, turning the stranger's lost mind into a weapon.

Sitting on a motel bed, Martin recites the Prine case down a phone line to an anonymous caller. The voice feeds him a target, giving him the name, trade, and address of a drug dealer named Gil Marsh.

Martin waits in the dark of another motel bathroom to ambush Vance, beating him brutally before driving him out of town at gunpoint.

In a flooded basement, Martin strangles Gil Marsh with a belt and snaps a photograph of the corpse. As Gil dies, he gasps a single word—"Elias"—which means nothing to Martin, who changes into the dead man’s suit, takes his keys, and drives off in his sports car.

Corinne has a friend at the vehicle registry run the registration off Martin’s note, then hands him a printed sheet naming Roy Mercer.

In the derelict building, Roy confronts Martin, revealing that Gil was innocent, that revenge happened a year ago, and that the story Martin tells down the phone is his own life. Unwilling to hold a truth that leaves him with nothing, Martin burns Gil's photographs, writes *he is lying to you* across Roy’s picture, and copies down Roy’s licence plate.

Martin lures Roy back to the same derelict building on a pretext, puts a bullet through the officer's head, and photographs the corpse, satisfied that his written note was right.

They had met at the end of the rail line, breaking into a shuttered shore house during a seaside party. For two years, their love unfolded across small rooms and cold weather: lying on frozen river ice, watching noodle house steam condense on glass, and sitting low in drive-ins with the speaker turned off. But the connection curdled into bitter recrimination over her drinking and his stony withholding. When she returned at two in the morning having dented his car, their final violent row ended with her packing a bag and walking out for good.

Tobias woke weeks later with a dull headache and a strange flatness. There was nobody in his head who had not been there two years ago, and he moved through his empty flat unaware that a whole chapter of his life had been excised overnight.

Desperate to erase him, Ivy had hired a shabby clinic to strip every trace of Tobias from her mind. When Tobias later visited her bookshop to make amends, she looked straight through him like a customer, flirting blithely with a young clerk named Peck. Devastated after Nina and Grady showed him the clinic’s form letter, Tobias went straight to Dr. Hallam to demand the same procedure, filling carrier bags with hairslides, mugs, and paper scraps so the technicians could map the attached memories.

Skipping work on an impulse he could not explain, Tobias boarded a northbound train. He walked out onto the frozen beach at the end of the line and found a woman with dyed hair already standing there, drawn by the same phantom pull.

In Tobias's flat, technicians Dell and Peck set up the equipment over the sleeping patient, Peck quietly pocketing the bagged keepsakes to use on Ivy later. Inside his own head, Tobias watched the ugliest recent memories dissolve first—the arguments, the silences, the slamming door. But as the machine reached the moments he loved, he panicked and tried to hide Ivy, smuggling her into childhood kitchens and unmapped places where the clinic's beam could not trace her.

They drove back to the city together, talking with a fluid, terrifying ease. Outside her building, she invited him up to her flat for a drink as though continuing a conversation started years ago.

Outside Tobias’s head, Dell and Rosa got high on his bed, completely failing to notice his brain map careening off the rails. Dr. Hallam arrived at three in the morning to re-map the procedure. When Rosa kissed Hallam in the hallway, his wife arrived behind him and calmly revealed that Rosa’s own past affair with the director had been erased by the clinic long ago.

Disillusioned by the revelation, Rosa quit her job, emptying the clinic's filing cabinets and mailing the original logs, object lists, and recorded intake tapes back to every patient on the books.

Inside the very last surviving memory—the dark, broken shore house from the night they first met—Tobias stood in a room whose walls were dissolving into white fog. Before she vanished entirely, Ivy turned to him in the fading darkness and told him to meet her at the beach.

Two heavy brown envelopes arrived on Ivy’s landing. Sitting on the stairwell steps, Tobias and Ivy listened to the tapes of their own bitter voices explaining why they wanted each other erased. Ivy ran down the hall in tears, paused, and came back. Staring at the evidence of their past, they agreed to try again anyway.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett Rusk sat in a lawyer’s office while the banker Barrow listed the vast holdings of his estate. Out of all his vast wealth, Emmett declared he wished only to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion, believing it might be fun. He moved his bed directly into the newspaper offices, installed his manager Marsh and his loyal friend Devlin on either side of him, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Shortly after, he bought away the entire staff of the rival paper across the street by offering higher pay, throwing a lavish party complete with a brass band and a chorus line.

Following a buying trip abroad for statuary, Emmett returned engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. Before long, a run of breakfast-table scenes charted their marriage cooling into silence behind separate newspapers. Splashed by a cab on a street corner, Emmett laughed at the mud on his coat alongside a shopgirl named Nora Kell and began visiting her rooms in secret.

Midway through Emmett’s campaign for governor, the political party boss Halloran brought Adele directly to Nora’s rooms, threatening total exposure unless Emmett withdrew. Emmett refused to back down, lost the election, and watched his marriage collapse while Devlin asked to be transferred to another city.

Emmett married Nora next and forced her into an opera career despite her having no voice. Her debut was a disaster; Devlin got drunk rather than write a kind review and fell asleep over half a paragraph, so Emmett finished the savage critique himself, printed it, and fired his friend. Only when Nora swallowed poison in a dark room did Emmett finally allow her to stop singing.

He locked Nora away at Silvermount, a half-finished palace where she spent her days working jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a vast empty hall. Following a joyless beach picnic and a bitter quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him. In a rage, Emmett wrecked her bedroom until he found a small glass snow globe. He murmured "Bluebell" and carried it past endless facing mirrors that reflected his aging form. Alone in his bed, Emmett died with the word "Bluebell" on his lips, dropping the globe to shatter on the floor.

In a screening room, the reporter Nash watched a nine-minute newsreel obituary recapping Emmett's public life, which ended without explaining his final word. Sent to uncover its meaning, Nash sought out Nora in a seaside nightclub at four in the afternoon, but the drunken former singer turned him away before he could finish his question.

Nash retired to a library to read Barrow’s written memoir. 

Decades earlier, in a western mining boarding house, a lodger who could not pay his board had left behind a defaulted mine deed that proved enormously rich. Emmett’s mother sat at the kitchen table signing her son and the fortune over to Barrow, while his father objected from the doorway and was ignored. Outside in the deep snow, young Emmett drove his wooden sled straight into Barrow’s stomach, but he was taken east away from his parents regardless.

Having finished the memoir, Nash interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the old butler Colm before putting his notebook away, concluding that no single word could ever explain a life. Meanwhile, as workmen cleared Silvermount's halls of crates, a laborer picked up a small wooden sled marked Blue

Four adults, a baby, and a rottweiler named Tigre shared a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch, watching his brother Nestor’s wife, Alma, move quietly through the kitchen. When Nestor hid his face behind a scarf to rob a night chemist and came home to beat Alma across the floor, Ruben began urging her to run away with him. Money was the only barrier, but Ruben found a way: discovering Tigre killed other dogs on sight, he entered the rottweiler into underground dogfights, winning steadily alongside his friend Pipo. Desperate to speed their escape, Ruben paid two thugs to jump Nestor. The plan backfired; Nestor emerged from the hospital, guessed the truth, and vanished with Alma, the baby, and all of Ruben’s hidden cash. Left with nothing but the ring, Ruben kept fighting the dog until the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the middle of a match. Ruben plunged a knife into Chaco’s chest and fled into the night with Pipo. Months later, after Nestor was shot dead during a bank robbery, Ruben stood beside his brother’s open grave and begged Alma one last time to leave with him. She looked at him with empty eyes and refused.

Across the city, model Celine Vaz moved into a high-rise flat bought by her lover Hector, who had abandoned his wife and daughters at a birthday party to be with her. From her living room window, Celine’s face stared back at her from a massive billboard across the street. But her new life shattered in a split second when a speeding truck ran a red light and crushed her car. She woke in a hospital ward, her leg bound in a cage of steel pins, asking only for her lapdog Chispa. Unbeknownst to her, Chispa had slipped through a hole in the floorboards of the empty flat. As Hector spent days tearing up the apartment with a crowbar searching for the whining dog, Celine’s leg went gangrenous above the knee. Surgeons amputated the limb. By the time she returned home, the billboard across the street had been stripped bare, leaving only a blank metal frame.

At the junction where Ruben had run the red light and slammed into Celine’s car, a vagrant named Cardo—a former guerrilla turned contract killer—had watched the smoke rise. Ignoring the human survivors, Cardo pulled the bleeding rottweiler from the wreckage and slipped away. In his yard of strays, Cardo nursed Tigre back to health, feeding the wounded beast by hand. His dark routine continued when a wealthy businessman named Elian hired him behind a church to murder his half-brother and partner, Sergio. Around the same time, Cardo stood at the perimeter of a cemetery, watching his estranged wife buried by a family who believed he had died decades ago. He secretly trailed his grown daughter, Perla, back to her apartment building. 

Returning to his yard one afternoon, Cardo found that Tigre had slaughtered every other stray in the pack. Cardo pressed a gun directly to the rottweiler’s forehead, but he found himself unable to pull the trigger. Instead of carrying out Elian's contract, Cardo abducted Sergio off the street and chained him to a bedframe in the yard. He then fetched Elian, brought the two brothers face to face, placed a loaded pistol on the floor between them, took payment from both, and walked away. 

Breaking into Perla’s apartment while she was at work, Cardo left a long, painful confession on her answering machine, revealing his identity and explaining his long absence before stealing a single framed photograph of her. Shaved and dressed in clean clothes, he left all his remaining money on her table. With nowhere left to turn, Cardo walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the edge of the city, followed closely by Tigre.

Nadir stood at the glass counter while his daughter Sahar translated. The gun dealer mocked Nadir’s heavy accent to an empty room, but Nadir paid and took the heavy pistol. Across town, outside an upscale restaurant, Trey and Kwame drew handguns on prosecutor Halstead and his wife Paula, stealing their luxury sedan. Hours later, on a dark road, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart. Boyle forced Renee against the bonnet, his hands trespassing up her skirt while Clay stood three feet away, frozen in silence, and Boyle’s partner Voss watched from the cruiser.

Before any of that night's wounds could heal, Officer Voss would pull his patrol car to the shoulder of a rain-slicked country road to pick up a young hitchhiker named Kwame. When Kwame reached into his pocket for something, Voss would panic, misread the motion, fire two bullets into him, and drive the body to a ditch before burning the car.

At the station the next morning, Voss asked his commander for a new car, claiming Boyle suffered from unbearable flatulence just to escape the racist officer. Meanwhile, Mateo worked on the Halsteads' front door. Paula stood at the top of the stairs, shouting to her husband that the tattooed locksmith would sell their new keys to gang members by morning. 

Mateo left and went straight to Nadir’s shop to repair the back lock. He warned Nadir that the door frame itself was rotten, but Nadir snapped at him, convinced Mateo was running a con. That afternoon, Boyle sat across a desk at a health insurance office, begging clerk Delia Frank for a referral for his dying father. Delia offered a flat refusal, driving Boyle to rage.

That night, thieves kicked down Nadir’s door exactly as warned, looting his stock and defacing the walls. When the adjuster reviewed the claim, the insurer refused to pay because Nadir had ignored the structural warning. 

A crash echoed on a slip road soon after. Renee Hobart was trapped upside down in a burning vehicle. Crawling through shattered glass, Boyle—the man who had violated her—cut her seatbelt and dragged her to safety.

Trey and Kwame swept through the city in Halstead's car, striking a pedestrian named Pham between two parked vans. After a heated argument, they dumped his bleeding body outside a hospital entrance. Shortly after, police surrounded Clay Hobart as he tried to unlock his own vehicle, mistaking him for a carjacker. Voss intervened, talking his fellow officers down before triggers were pulled. Clay then drove off at blinding speed with Trey trapped in his passenger seat, eventually pulling over on an empty verge and dumping Trey into the dark.

Desperate and ruined, Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with his handgun hidden beneath his coat. When Mateo emerged, Nadir raised the barrel and screamed. Little Rosie ran off the porch into Mateo’s arms just as Nadir pulled the trigger. The shot was deafening, but neither father nor child bled; Sahar had secretly purchased blanks. Nadir fell to his knees, convinced the girl was an angel sent to save him.

The rain turned cold along that deserted country road where Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking. Misinterpreting the youth’s movement as he reached into his pocket, Voss shot Kwame dead, dumped his body by the roadside, and torched the vehicle. 

Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the scene. Approaching the corpse face down in the mud, Reece froze, recognizing his brother Kwame’s shoes. At home, Reece’s mother collapsed onto the kitchen floor, weeping and blaming Reece for never searching for his brother.

In her grand house, Paula fell down the staircase. Lying injured until her housekeeper Alba found her, Paula wept in the ambulance, telling Alba she was her only friend.

Trey later purchased Pham’s abandoned van cheap. Opening the rear doors, he found two dozen trafficked migrants locked in the dark. Instead of selling them, Trey drove to the docks, handed them his cash, and set them free.

First snow began to fall. At a crowded junction, two cars collided, and both drivers leaped out, shouting abuse before even looking at the damage.

Helicopters swept low through the night sky, spraying poison across every neighbourhood to eradicate crop pests. Beneath their hum, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, got ready for an upcoming dinner party with quiet, brewing resentment.

Across town, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake for a young boy named Charlie Rill. Later that week, as Charlie walked to school, a waitress named Rhona struck him with her car. The boy insisted he was unhurt and walked home, but he soon collapsed into a coma. His parents, Grant and Elaine, began a desperate hospital vigil. Grant’s estranged father Duff turned up in the corridor and confessed to an affair from decades ago.

With the birthday cake uncollected and unpaid for, Otto began making anonymous menacing phone calls to the Rill house in the middle of the night. Across the city, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu sat beside her, quietly seething.

Seeking an escape, Stu and three friends drove out to fish and found a young woman's body face down in the mountain river. They tethered the corpse to the bank with a line around her ankle and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone. When Vern returned home and told his wife Iris, a party clown, she was disgusted by what the men had done.

Meanwhile, the singer Vida performed nightly in a club while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home. Around the same time, Officer Rowe, who was cheating on his wife Peg with a woman called Nan, abandoned the family dog on a distant road to cover one of his lies. Nan’s ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, discovered she had a new man and sawed every piece of her furniture to splinters.

While the Hartigans were away, Ike and Dot house-sat for them and took photographs of Dot made up as a beaten corpse in the hallway. When the Hartigans finally hosted their dinner party, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair, prompting Neil to make a bitter public scene.

The following morning, Charlie died in his hospital room. Grant and Elaine drove straight to the bakery to confront Otto over the harassing calls. Realizing who they were, the baker broke down, fed them warm bread, and grieved with them.

That afternoon, Bee found her mother asleep in her chair as usual. Bee walked out to the garage, closed the door, and killed herself with the car engine running.

Hours later, during a picnic in the hills, Cheryl made an offhand comment that pushed Stu over the edge; he picked up a rock and smashed her head in.

Shortly after, a sudden tremor shook the entire city for eleven seconds. By nightfall, every wreck, every broken home, and every death were folded neatly into a single evening news bulletin.

For six months, severe insomnia reduced my existence to a pale, wakeful fog. The only relief I found was attending church hall support groups for diseases I did not have, crying in the arms of the dying until emotional exhaustion bought me a single night of sleep. Then Ada Vey started showing up. Her obvious, exaggerated faking made my own deceit painfully clear, destroying my catharsis and leaving me sleepless once again.

Months later, down in the damp concrete service stairwell of a target tower, Rex Marrow would beat me mercilessly down flight after flight. In that dark stairwell, I would finally understand that the gun Rex held against my head was held in my own right hand. To eliminate the phantom taking over my life, I would force the cold steel barrel between my teeth, angle it sideways, and fire a bullet directly through my own cheek.

Before any of that happened, I was on a night flight sitting beside Rex Marrow, a charismatic soap salesman who talked passionately about how consumer culture owned us. I pocketed his card. Shortly after, a mysterious explosion destroyed my flat, scattering my catalogue furniture across the pavement. Homeless, I phoned Rex, and he took me in to live in a sprawling derelict house at the edge of the industrial district.

One night outside a bar, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody on the asphalt, feeling more alive than ever. What began as two men brawling soon hardened into a structured basement club with its own strict rules, attracting endless rows of men eager to fight.

When Ada overdosed on medication, Rex brought her back to the derelict house. The two of them began a loud, relentless affair, their voices echoing through the floorboards while I lay rigid downstairs in agonizing envy. To finance his growing enterprise, Rex rendered fat stolen from cosmetic surgery clinic waste bins into high-end soap, selling it back to luxury department stores at eighty dollars a bar. In the kitchen, he poured wet lye onto the back of my hand, burning the flesh and pinning me down, refusing to let me retreat into meditation or count breaths as the chemical seared my skin.

Using my smashed, bruised face as leverage, I walked into my office and blackmailed my employer into paying me a regular salary to stay away. Rex used those funds to forge the fight club into a militant organization called Havoc. He filled the derelict house with shaven recruits who followed orders without question and vandalized corporate property under the cover of night.

During a rainy drive, Rex took his hands off the steering wheel, allowed the car to drift into oncoming traffic, and let it roll into a ditch. When I regained consciousness in the wreckage, Rex had vanished. Not long after, a Havoc

Across the sea, his cousin Marv called with explicit instructions: bring the stone straight over without delay. Back in the city, Grigor the Nail tipped Solly off about a busy bookmaker's shop, while simultaneously tipping off two pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, to rob Solly at that exact location.

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their contract fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. The negotiation turned violent when a bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked Sam out cold over the deal, leaving Halloway without a man for gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Cornered, Halloway was forced to put Finn in the fight instead, promising a dangerous Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Upon landing in the city, Solly delivered the massive diamond directly to the fence Hersch for safekeeping before heading toward the bookmaker's to place his bet. When Ike, Benno, and their associate Tulley bungled the robbery inside, they panicked, taking Solly's arm along with his case before being chased off by Grigor. Shortly after, at the underground fight venue, Finn ignored his instructions and knocked his opponent out cold in the first round; Coldstone lost a fortune on the outcome and took his fury out on Halloway.

Elsewhere, Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took custody of both the men and the stone they had managed to retrieve.

High above the wet street, an old man stood by an open window, looking down at the red and blue reflections flickering across the asphalt. He spoke quietly to the young man standing in the shadow behind him. "Nothing survives time," he said, resting his hand on the sill. "Not love, not fury, not memory. It isn't a tragedy, boy, just a fact."

Directly below the window, police officers hauled Cort and Jonah out of the basement entrance, forcing them through the murmuring crowd. Cort dragged his heels, weeping from the agony in his shattered arm, while Jonah moved in dead silence, staring blindly at the wet pavement as handcuffs bound his blood-slicked wrists behind his back.

Minutes earlier, inside the suffocating gloom of the Pit, Jonah had torn a heavy red fire extinguisher from the wall. He brought it down again and again into the face of a man pinned against the bar, long after the stranger had stopped moving, smashing bone to pulp. Just a few feet away in the shadows, the real Adder stood with his back pressed against an iron pillar, calmly sipping a gin and tonic as he watched the wrong man die for his crime.

Before the violence erupted, Cort had stalked through the flashing strobe light of the basement club, grabbing men by the collar and peering into their faces. Half-blind with rage and alcohol, he had seized the wrong shoulder. The man had turned without a word, caught Cort by the forearm, and twisted his elbow until the joint snapped like dry timber.

They had been steered to the club by two strangers who had stepped out of an alley doorway. For a crumpled stack of bank notes, the touts had sold Cort and Jonah a name—the Adder—and pointed them toward the low doorway of the Pit.

The two men had been searching for a target ever since stepping out of a house party half an hour prior. Still breathless and laughing from the noise inside, Cort and Jonah had halted on the sidewalk as paramedics wheeled a gurney past. Under the glare of the flashing blue light, they recognized the bloodied face resting beneath the shock blanket.

Lise lay broken on the concrete floor of a pedestrian underpass long before the ambulance arrived. The Adder had dragged her into the dark corner, violently raping her and striking her head against the stone walls with methodical, unhurried cruelty. At the far mouth of the tunnel, a lone passerby had paused, caught sight of the assault, panicked, and backed away into the shadows without uttering a sound.

Lise had stepped down into that subterranean passage only to avoid crossing four lanes of speeding traffic. Halfway down the damp, tiled tunnel, she had stopped dead in her tracks, coming face-to-face with a pimp known as the Adder as he held a transsexual woman by her hair, beating her bruised face with his fists.

She was walking home alone because the party had turned sour. Hours before, Cort had gotten recklessly drunk and high, abandoning Lise to pursue other women across the crowded apartment. Sickened by his carelessness, Lise had gathered her coat and left by herself.

Yet the evening had started with laughter. On the underground train ride there, Lise, Cort, and Jonah stood swaying together in the crowded carriage, cheerfully teasing one another about sex, Cort’s drinking habits, and their shared history, secure in the easy warmth of people who expected tomorrow to be identical to today.

Before the sun set, the afternoon had been pure tranquility. In the public park, sprinklers whirred over sweet-smelling cut grass as children ran laughing through the fine spray. Lise lay on her side on a blanket with a paperback book she wasn't reading, resting her hand flat against her stomach.

That morning, alone in the quiet flat, Lise had sat on the edge of the porcelain bathtub holding a plastic stick in both hands. She looked down at the positive result and let a slow, private smile spread across her face, treasuring the secret she had not yet shared with anyone.

Earlier still, morning light had streamed through thin curtains into the bedroom. Lise lay in bed beside Cort, softly describing a recurring dream she kept having about walking into a dark red tunnel, while the two of them traded lazy, affectionate insults about her ex-boyfriend Jonah, completely at ease in the quiet safety of a morning that had not yet been undone.

Emlyn stood in Wilder’s hallway, unspooling his heavy wool scarf with deliberate slowness. He smiled faintly and informed his oldest friend that he had known about the affair for four full years—ever since Odile had confessed during their trip abroad. Besides, Emlyn added with mild contempt, he had never thought much of Wilder’s letters anyway.

Earlier that evening, frantic and shaken, Wilder had snatched up the telephone receiver in a panic. He dialed Emlyn’s home, his voice trembling as he begged his friend to come to the house at once.

That afternoon, in the shadowed corner of a quiet bar, Odile had let slip a stray piece of news over her glass. She casually mentioned that Emlyn had spent the past year publishing a novelist whom Wilder represented, a hack writer whom both men had quietly detested for years.

Just before that revelation, sitting in the same velvet booth, Odile had summoned Wilder to break her grand news: her marriage was finally over. She explained that she had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband, thoroughly convinced she was delivering the very first complete account of their long betrayal.

Two years prior to that drink in the bar, Wilder and Odile stood among half-packed boxes in the flat they rented. Deciding the parallel household had turned into an exhausting chore, they split the stack of crockery between them and surrendered the lease to the landlord.

Months before the lease was given up, dinner at the married couple’s house had carried its own subtle cruelty. Sitting at the head of the table, Emlyn and Wilder traded spirited memories of racquet games and schoolboy sport, locked in an exclusive male rapport until Odile had no part in the conversation at all.

Earlier that season, Emlyn had dragged Wilder through a long, boozy restaurant lunch. Emlyn drank heavily through three courses, constantly baiting the book agent about the mediocrity of contemporary fiction, yet never once dropping his guard or mentioning what he had learned.

Before that lunch, Odile had returned to the rented rooms straight from the railway station. She hung her coat, sat beside Wilder, and said nothing whatever about her journey abroad, letting the long afternoon pass exactly as all the others had.

In a hotel room overseas, days before that quiet afternoon, Odile had finally collapsed under the weight of her secret and confessed. Emlyn had absorbed the truth without rising from his chair, remarking dryly that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

An hour earlier, in the bright marble lobby of that same foreign hotel, Emlyn had gestured toward an envelope resting on the mail tray. He asked his wife about the letter held for her at the desk, noting quietly that it was addressed in a hand he recognised instantly.

Before that journey abroad, inside the quiet rooms, Odile had told Wilder she was carrying her husband’s child. Neither lover suggested retreat; instead, they decided then and there that the rented space would go on exactly as before.

Months before the pregnancy, they had scouted the quiet districts together to find those rooms. They bought armfuls of fresh linen and painted plates, determined to give their illicit affair a domestic life and household of its own.

It had begun years earlier, amidst the dull roar of a party downstairs in Emlyn’s house. While the guests drank and laughed in the rooms below, Wilder had led his closest friend’s wife up the dark stairs into a quiet bedroom, taking her hand to tell her how lovely she was.

He is born in a grey, small industrial town, growing into a frail and peculiar child entirely unsuited for the demands of the world.

His father hurls him into the deep end of a municipal swimming pool to teach him to swim. The boy offers no resistance, sinking directly to the concrete bottom and lying on the tile floor, finding the heavy water peaceful.

Without any proper combat training, he is conscripted into the army as a chaplain’s assistant and shipped overseas on a crowded transport.
